featured_reviews.name: Mrs. SHARADA KADAM
featured_reviews.review_text:
Hello, my name is Sharada Rakesh Kadam. My mother works in this hospital as a helper (maushi), and she always says that all the doctors here are very good. Based on her recommendation,Today I visited Paramount Hospital today to consult a dermatologist, Dr. Prateek Oswal.
When my turn came and I entered the cabin for my check-up, it seems that the receptionist had informed the doctor that I am the daughter of a staff member. On hearing this, the doctor became angry and said, “Whoever it is, I am not going to give any concession,” and abruptly hung up the phone. After that, the way my consultation was handled was extremely disappointing—something I could never have imagined. For a moment, I was even scared to ask him any questions.
I paid the full consultation fee as asked, and I had absolutely no issue paying it. However, the doctor should have at least clarified or spoken to me before reacting in such a manner.
I truly regret visiting based on my mother’s recommendation. I am a tax consultant by profession and have worked with reputed doctors in Mumbai. I have had direct professional interactions with well-known doctors from hospitals like SevenHills, Hinduja, and Surya Hospital, and I still have their direct contact numbers. Even today, if I have any concerns regarding my children or my husband, I can directly reach out to them. However, I have never had such a poor experience with any doctor before.
My mother continues to work there due to her financial condition, and she has no choice. I understand her situation. But after this experience, I will never visit this hospital again. This entire incident was extremely unprofessional and disappointing.

--------Thank you for responding to my review so quickly—I truly appreciate it.
I understand that my mother is an elderly woman, and she may sometimes ask for a discount. However, even if I had been charged ₹800 as a consultation fee, I would have paid it without any issue. My main concern was simply to get proper treatment for my skin infection. There was absolutely no need for such a reaction.
I would also like to mention that the hospitals I referred to earlier---------are places where I have known doctors personally since 2008. Till date, they have never charged me a consultation fee. So, this is not about the fee at all; it is about the way the situation was handled. The reaction was unnecessary and could have been avoided.
Honestly, I always pray to God that I have minimal need to visit doctors in life. During my consultation, when I asked Dr. Oswal whether I should use any normal anti-aging creams—as I am 40 years old and do not currently use anything on my skin—his response was quite unsatisfactory.

Anyway, I shared my experience as it happened. I sincerely hope that my mother receives respect at her workplace. Earlier, she worked at Dhanvantari Hospital, where everyone treated her very well. Yesterday’s experience, however, was quite different for me.

Thank you once again for your response. 🙏🙏🙏

I had one of the worst experiences at this hospital. Except for Dr. Shams Alam, who was genuinely professional, the rest of the staff were extremely disappointing. Overall, I strongly advise others not to consider this hospital for treatment. There are many better and more humane healthcare options available. Please avoid Apex if you value your health and dignity.

featured_reviews.review_text:
Outside India currently and had my wife visit her clinic as she is currently pregnant. She had the most disturbing experience speaking with Dr. Vaishali Ghiya, the primary obstetrician at Carewel.

We had first visited Carewel 3 years ago for our first child. For the delivery, however, I had to take my wife to the hospital at 3 AM and there was no transport available. So we decided to go to the second hospital that we had registered in which was closer to where we live.

My wife had the Carewel file from her previous pregnancy which she carried  with her yesterday while visiting Carewel hospital. Dr Vaishali Ghiya was clearly upset that we chose to go to the second hospital on our list last time.

She made so many nasty comments that my wife almost cried. It's a shame that someone so educated has such a vile tongue. Some of the comments that she made are:

1. You guys are so poor. Maybe you cannot afford treatment here.
2. You should go to a government hospital
3. I will charge Rs 1500 to give an IV. Can you afford that? Should I start the treatment?
4. Why did you come here now? Why didn’t you go to the second hospital? Did something go wrong there?
5. Why are you coming when you are so far along?
6. There are two medicines, one for 1800, one for 2400 which one can you afford?

My wife and MIL, being kind and reserved, took these comments in silence. But is this any way for a doctor to talk to the patients? What kind of an example does it set for those working under her? Will nurses and wardboys also have the same attitude when a patient is admitted?

For perspective, my wife and I have a combined income of over 36LPA and, if we wanted, we could go to the most expensive hospital in Mumbai. We are shocked to see such an attitude from a doctor that treats women when they are at their most vulnerable. Honestly, I think we dodged a bullet here.

The irony is that my modestly dressed wife and I could pay for 12 deliveries at Carewel and still have money left over from our monthly income.

Update: I’ve experienced both private consultation and general OPD at Holy Spirit Hospital, and overall, it has been a bad experience.

The campus itself is beautiful and well maintained. Online appointment booking is smooth, while offline booking starts at 7:30 am and doctors typically begin consultations from around 8:30 am.

The private consultation experience (ENT, in my case) was genuinely good. The doctor gave adequate time, listened patiently, and the interaction felt reassuring and professional. However, this comes at a cost, as the visit including diagnostics ended up in the range of ₹3,000–4,000.

The general OPD experience was very bad. The charges are in the range of ₹400-700.

Earlier I had positive experiences with  Gastroenterology and Surgery. I was very much impressed with the surgeon, but his opinion was outrightly dismissed by 3 other senior surgeons and physicians. I realised he kept focussing on a know problem which wasn't connected to my pain.  Gastroenterologist doesn't do any physical examination to understand the location of pain or confirm hemorrhoids. Seems, he only checks you during pricey colonoscopy and endoscopy procedures.

My experience with General Medicine and Urology OPD was disappointing. In these departments, the main doctor and an assistant doctor sit at the same small table and consult two different patients simultaneously.

In General Medicine OPD, there were up to four patients along with their attendants inside the same room at once—one with the main doctor, one with the assistant, one waiting behind the doctor, and another at the entrance being triaged for blood pressure and weight. That easily translates to 8–10 people in a single consultation room. There is no space for discussion, questions, nuance, or privacy. The doctor barely had time for eye contact, let alone a detailed conversation or examination.

In the Urology OPD, I could speak to the actual doctor only after the assistant doctor felt I was not convinced. While I do not question the competence of junior doctors, as a patient it feels unfair when you do not get adequate time with the consultant you booked.

I guess this is the truth of INR 400-700 consultations. I sincerely hope the PRO and hospital administration take note of these inconsistencies, especially given Holy Spirit’s reputation as an esteemed institution.

featured_reviews.review_text:
SBS Hospital claims to provide “world-class medical services at an affordable price,” but our experience was far from this promise.
My mother-in-law was admitted twice (9–17 December and 20–23 January) under Dr. Ankita Chauhan for severe UTI and electrolyte imbalance. While the doctor was competent, the hospital administration and billing practices were extremely disappointing.
During the first admission, Post depositing ₹20,000, the hospital bill reached ₹89,000. This included ₹200 per use of a finger oximeter, charged 17 times (₹3,400) for a basic device that costs under ₹1,000. Medicines and IVs were billed separately (≈₹50,000) with only a 10% discount, pathology tests were outsourced at high rates, and daily payments were demanded from both hospital and pharmacy, treating relatives like potential defaulters.
During the second admission, patient comfort was ignored—AC switched off, no fan, and repeated requests to nurses and resident doctors were ignored for two days, until strong protest.
On discharge day (23 January), despite the doctor clearly instructing that we should not be charged for the day, the receptionist—while remaining outwardly calm and polite—kept repeatedly pressuring and subtly threatening us with additional charges if payment was delayed. Even after explaining our situation, reminders continued (“it’s already 3 p.m.”, “you’ll be charged”, "Its already 4:30"), creating unnecessary stress.  We had informed her we did not have the money and my Sis in law will make the payment. (She already has 2 patients to take care of 1 is a dialysis patient and other is a parkinsons patient.) That was the breaking point.  We were not going to abscond.  When me and my husband finally raised our voice, she said, “Ma’am, why are you shouting? And told my husband that There are cameras.”  We were angry only when she showed no empathy, patience and was repeatedly after us.    Only after admin intervention did the situation de-escalate.
Speaking softly does not equal empathy. The hospital staff needs serious training in humanity and patient/relative handling, not just protocols.
Please do not blindly trust online ratings—I personally witnessed reception staff helping non–tech-savvy relatives submit reviews.
The only saving grace of this hospital is Dr. Ankita Chauhan and the Mavshis.
For reference (second admission):
Hospital bill: ₹43,000 (after ₹1,300 discount,  1200 for the oxymeter and 100 to round off the amount)
Pharmacy bill: ₹14,500
Due to mounting expenses and as the patient was stable, we opted for DAMA, with injections continued at home.  The 1 star rating is because, we are unable to submit the review without providing any rating.

featured_reviews.name: khyati malhotra
featured_reviews.review_text:
While the doctors are competent and unfortunately, the experience beyond that has been deeply disappointing.

Across multiple visits over the last 5 years, every 6 months to 1 year prices increase.
However nursing talent keeps decreasing.
I have encountered young and seemingly undertrained nursing staff missing medication doses, procuring incorrect dosages, and struggling with basic communication due to language barriers.

What makes the experience even more frustrating is the administrative burden. Nearly every visit seems to require a follow-up visit solely for cashless authorization formalities. The staff at the TPA desk and those coordinating with the nursing teams often appear overworked, overwhelmed, and visibly frustrated—unfortunately, patients end up bearing the brunt of this dysfunction.

The 13th floor is scorned even by the nursing staff. On previous occasions we have been advised off the record to move to 12/14th floor because 13th floor is poorly managed. We have seen unclean rooms, dust deposits as if not cleaned for days, a floor so dull and lacking staff you can shoot a horror movie there!
If this is the standard at one of the region’s most awarded hospitals, it genuinely raises concerns about the broader healthcare experience elsewhere.

featured_reviews.name: Nirajkumar Chhangani
featured_reviews.review_text:
Admitted senior citizen patient experienced inefficiencies twice.

Untrained nurses:
hardly any experience, makes, adminsters saline drip and forgets to take out, checks BP without stethoscope, no regular checks on patient. No keeping track of appointments of x-ray, ct scan etc.
Measures and notes 90/50 BP for a high BP patient as normal !
Communication issues. Standard answers for any query.

Administration:
1. Too much process but too little staff to handle the load. So, even for admission or any procedure related forms, you end up waiting for 1 to 2 hours after taking token.

2. TPA / cashles - At admission policy details are asked but not informed that there those are not being used to initiate mediclaim. So, you may lose one day thinking they might have initiated.
Then you come to know about token thing for TPA desk, and heavy form filling, and printouts etc.

3. For every subsequent query or work, you have to wait for endless queues. If aksed for senior persons, reply is negative. No other supervisor/senior only the front desks.

4. Cashless is joke - because you will be asked to deposit almost 80 to 90% upfront before any procedure. Out if this 10% is refunded 2 to 3 months later.

Diagnostics:
Same endless queues, you get appointment for 12 pm. Patient without any food since morning. Waiting outside the labs, the number comes at 4pm ! Even seen ICU patient waiting for so long - how can one normalize such process ? If you want reports, again you will have to run from pillar to post - not given to patient directly.

The doctor you opt for, may give attention for the procedure he is supposed to perform, after that its all lose ends, no cohesive treatment, and no easy access to doctors.

However, we would like to share a few suggestions that may help improve patient comfort and care further:

- In shared wards, TV volume is often kept very high by other patients/attendants, which can disturb rest and recovery. Better monitoring of noise levels would be helpful.
- During the shift from ICU to ward, there was swelling noticed in the patient’s hand, possibly due to negligency in handling which unfortunately was not identified immediately.
- Medicine administration and checks sometimes required repeated reminders. We felt the need to stay highly vigilant and repeatedly request reviews/checks.
- During nurse shift changes, there were occasions where the incoming staff did not seem fully aware of the patient’s details and ongoing requirements.
- It would also be reassuring if resident doctors could occasionally visit and console or update patients/families during night hours as well.
